cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Why is economics a social science, and how does its methodology differ from the natural sciences?
cards.back:
Economics applies the scientific method — observation, hypothesis formation, testing, refinement — to human behaviour and societies.

Unlike the natural sciences it cannot run controlled laboratory experiments, so economists build models resting on simplifying assumptions and test them against real-world data. Different assumptions can lead economists to different conclusions from the same data.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Define ceteris paribus, and explain why economists rely on it.
cards.back:
Ceteris paribus — a Latin phrase meaning ‘all other things being equal’ or ‘all other factors held constant’.

It lets economists isolate the causal relationship between two variables — the law of demand holds ceteris paribus. In reality ‘other things’ are rarely constant, a key limitation of economic models.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Define positive statements.
cards.back:
Positive statements — objective statements that describe 'what is', 'what was', or 'what will be' in the economy.

They are based on empirical evidence and can be tested or falsified — "the UK's inflation rate is 3.2%" can be checked against the data.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Define normative statements.
cards.back:
Normative statements — subjective statements that express an opinion or a value judgement about what ought to be.

They rest on opinions, ethics and beliefs, so they cannot be tested or proven false — "the government should increase spending on the NHS" is a matter of debate, not data.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Define a value judgement, and explain how value judgements influence economic policy.
cards.back:
Value judgement — a view about what is morally or subjectively important. These judgements underpin all normative statements.

AQA emphasises that people's views on the best option are influenced both by the positive consequences of different decisions and by moral and political judgements — for example, whether a government prioritises efficiency or equality.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: What is the central purpose of economic activity? Distinguish needs from wants.
cards.back:
The central purpose of economic activity is the production of goods and services to satisfy needs and wants.

Needs — basic requirements for human survival, such as food, water and shelter. Wants — desires for goods and services that improve quality of life, such as entertainment and travel.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: State the three key economic decisions every economy must make.
cards.back:
• What to produce — which goods and services, given consumer demand and available resources.
  • How to produce — the production methods, technology and resource mix.
  • Who is to benefit — how the goods and services produced are distributed among the population.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Name and define the four factors of production.
cards.back:
• Land — natural resources, e.g. oil, wood.
  • Labour — human effort, e.g. baristas in a coffee shop.
  • Capital — man-made resources used in production, e.g. printers, laptops.
  • Enterprise — risk-taking to start or expand a business.

All four are combined to produce goods (tangible) and services (intangible).

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Match each factor of production to its factor reward.
cards.back:
• Land → rent
  • Labour → wages
  • Capital → interest
  • Enterprise → profit

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Why is the environment a scarce resource? Distinguish renewable from non-renewable resources.
cards.back:
The environment provides essential goods and services — clean air, water, fertile land — and overconsumption can leave it degraded, harming future economic activity, so it must be managed sustainably.

Non-renewable resources cannot be replaced once used (fossil fuels, minerals). Renewable resources replenish naturally (forests, fish stocks) but can still become scarce if overused or mismanaged.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Define scarcity — the fundamental economic problem.
cards.back:
Scarcity — when there are finite resources (e.g., land, labour, capital) but infinite human wants and needs.

Because of scarcity, choices must be made about how to allocate limited resources between competing uses — economics is the study of how those choices are made.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Define opportunity cost.
cards.back:
Opportunity cost — the value of the next best alternative foregone when making an economic decision.

It measures the real cost of any choice: the opportunity cost of a government spending more on healthcare is the education or defence spending given up.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how does scarcity lead to opportunity cost for every economic agent?
cards.back:
Resources are finite while wants are unlimited, so there is scarcity. Scarcity forces every agent to choose between competing uses of resources, and every choice sacrifices the next best alternative — an opportunity cost.

Consumer: a video game bought is a cinema ticket foregone. Producer: a factory making cars cannot make bicycles. Government: more healthcare spending means less for education or defence.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Define a production possibility frontier (PPF).
cards.back:
Production possibility frontier — a curve that shows the maximum potential output combinations of two goods or services an economy can achieve when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed.

The axes are typically capital goods and consumer goods; the AQA specification calls these production possibility diagrams.

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Interpret the points on a production possibility diagram: on, inside and outside the frontier.
cards.back: Points on the frontier (A, C, D, B) are productively efficient — all resources fully and efficiently used. Point E inside the frontier means unemployed or inefficiently used resources: more of both goods is possible at zero opportunity cost. Point F outside is currently unattainable with existing resources and technology. A movement along the frontier, such as C to D, shows the opportunity cost of producing more consumer goods.
cards.svgAlt: Concave production possibility frontier for capital and consumer goods with points A, C, D and B on the curve, E inside it and F outside it

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Show economic growth and decline on a production possibility diagram, with causes of each.
cards.back: An outward shift (PPF1 to PPF2) shows economic growth — an increase in the quantity or quality of the factors of production: immigration, new resource discoveries, better education and training, technological advance. An inward shift (PPF1 to PPF3) shows economic decline — natural disasters destroying capital, war, or long-term unemployment eroding skills.
cards.svgAlt: Three concentric production possibility frontiers: an outward shift to PPF2 showing growth and an inward shift to PPF3 showing decline

cards.topic: 1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem
cards.front: Why are all points on the PPF productively efficient, but not all allocatively efficient?
cards.back:
Every point on the frontier uses all resources fully — none are wasted — so each is productively efficient. But allocative efficiency requires the particular combination of goods that maximises society's welfare, and only one point on the frontier does that — and we cannot know exactly which.

We can still say allocative efficiency improves when more of one good is produced without less of the other — for example, moving from E inside the frontier to C on it.

cards.front: What does it mean for economic agents to act rationally, and what does each agent maximise?
cards.back:
Rationality — making the choice with the highest expected net benefit, in the agent's self-interest.

  • Consumers maximise utility.
  • Firms maximise profit.
  • Workers maximise net welfare from employment.
  • Governments maximise social welfare.

cards.front: Define utility, distinguishing total from marginal utility.
cards.back:
Utility — the satisfaction or happiness a consumer derives from consuming goods and services.

Total utility — the total satisfaction from consuming a given quantity. Marginal utility — the additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit.

cards.front: State the hypothesis of diminishing marginal utility, and its link to the demand curve.
cards.back:
As a consumer consumes more units of a good, the additional satisfaction (marginal utility) from each extra unit eventually falls.

AQA expects you to know that diminishing marginal utility supports a downward-sloping demand curve — extra units give less satisfaction, so consumers only buy more at lower prices. (The equi-marginal principle is not required.)

cards.front: Draw the total utility curve, and mark where marginal utility is zero.
cards.back: Total utility rises steeply for the first units, then at a decreasing rate as marginal utility diminishes. It is maximised where marginal utility is zero — the flat top between units 3 and 4. Beyond that, marginal utility is negative and total utility falls: a fifth slice of cake makes you worse off.
cards.svgAlt: Total utility curve rising at a decreasing rate to a flat maximum between quantities three and four, then falling to quantity five

cards.front: What does "marginal" mean in economics, and why is the margin important for decision making?
cards.back:
Marginal — the additional or incremental change resulting from one more unit of a good, service or resource.

Decisions are made at the margin: consumers compare the marginal utility of one more unit with the price they must pay; firms compare marginal revenue with marginal cost to decide whether producing another unit is profitable.

cards.front: Define information gaps and asymmetric information.
cards.back:
Information gaps — a situation where one party lacks the information needed to make an informed decision.

Asymmetric information — a situation where one party in a transaction has more or better information than the other.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how does asymmetric information lead to market failure?
cards.back:
One party knows more than the other, so the less-informed party cannot judge true value or quality. Their decisions no longer maximise utility or profit, resources are misallocated, and the result can be market failure.

Example: a used-car seller hides known defects; the buyer overpays and loses utility. AQA flags imperfect information as a potential source of market failure in its own right.

cards.front: Define bounded rationality.
cards.back: Bounded rationality — the idea that individuals are limited in their ability to make rational decisions due to a lack of information, time or ability to process information.

cards.front: Define bounded self-control.
cards.back:
Bounded self-control — the idea that individuals may not always act in their own best interests due to a lack of self control.

Example: knowing a gym habit pays off but failing to keep it — the reasoning behind commitment devices.

cards.front: Define anchoring bias.
cards.back:
Anchoring bias — the idea that individuals may be influenced by the first piece of information they receive when making a decision, even if it is not relevant or accurate.

Example: a £100 product discounted to £80 reads as a bargain, judged against the anchor rather than rivals' prices.

cards.front: Name the other behavioural biases in AQA's specification, beyond anchoring.
cards.back:
• Availability bias — judging by the information that comes to mind most easily.
  • Framing bias — swayed by how information is presented ('90% fat free' vs '10% fat').
  • Herding (social norms) — following others' choices rather than deciding independently.
  • Rules of thumb — habitual shortcuts that save effort but can miss better options.
  • Altruism — choices made to benefit others, not to maximise own utility.

cards.front: Contrast traditional and behavioural economic theory.
cards.back:
Traditional economic theory — the assumption that individuals are rational decision makers who endeavour to maximise their utility.

Behavioural economic theory — the assumption that individuals are not always rational decision makers and that their decisions may be influenced by a range of psychological and social factors, which may lead to them making decisions that do not maximise their utility.

cards.front: Define altruism, and explain why it matters in behavioural economics.
cards.back:
Altruism — the idea that individuals may make decisions that are not in their own best interests, but are intended to benefit others, e.g. donating to charity or volunteering.

Together with perceptions of fairness, altruism shows choices are not driven purely by self-interest — 'irrational' under traditional theory, yet it can produce positive outcomes such as social cohesion and a sense of community.

cards.front: Define a nudge.
cards.back: Nudges — a concept in behavioural economics that refers to subtle interventions or changes in the choice architecture that influence people's behaviour in a predictable way without restricting their freedom of choice.

cards.front: Give a real-world example of a nudge used in UK economic policy.
cards.back:
Workplace pension auto-enrolment (rolled out from 2012): the default was switched from opt-in to opt-out. Freedom of choice was untouched, but participation among eligible private-sector employees roughly doubled to nearly nine in ten.

Application point: changing the default exploited inertia — a textbook nudge working at national scale.

cards.front: Define choice architecture and framing.
cards.back:
Choice architecture / framing — the design of different ways in which choices can be presented to consumers to influence their decision-making and behaviour towards making rational decisions.

How options are laid out — order, wording, defaults — changes what people choose even when the options themselves are unchanged. Firms use it too: Netflix makes its premium plan the default at sign-up.

cards.front: Name and define AQA's three types of choice in choice architecture.
cards.back:
• Default choice — making the desired option the one automatically selected if the consumer does not make an active choice, e.g. organ-donation opt-out systems.
  • Restricted choice — limiting the number of options to simplify decisions and reduce choice overload, e.g. a simplified restaurant menu.
  • Mandated choice — requiring consumers to make the desired choice legally, e.g. third-party car insurance.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Define demand, and state the law of demand.
cards.back:
Demand — the quantity of a good/service consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price in a given time period. Desire alone is not demand: effective demand needs both willingness and ability to pay.

Law of demand — there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Distinguish a movement along the demand curve from a shift of it.
cards.back: A movement along the curve is caused only by a change in the good's own price — an extension when price falls, a contraction when it rises. A shift (D1 to D2) is caused by a non-price factor: real incomes (normal vs inferior goods), tastes and advertising, the price of substitutes or complements, or population changes.
cards.svgAlt: Demand curve shifting right from D1 to D2, raising quantity from Q1 to Q2 at price P1

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: State the formula for price elasticity of demand (PED), and how to interpret its value.
cards.back: PED is negative for a normal demand curve — classify on the magnitude: 0 = perfectly inelastic; between 0 and 1 = relatively inelastic; 1 = unitary; above 1 = relatively elastic; infinity = perfectly elastic.
cards.formulaHtml: PED=%ΔQD%ΔP\text{PED} = \frac{\%\Delta Q_D}{\%\Delta P}PED=%ΔP%ΔQD​​

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: A coffee shop raises the price of a latte from £3.00 to £3.60 and weekly sales fall from 500 to 450 cups. Calculate the PED, and state what happens to revenue.
cards.back:
%Δ QD = −50 ÷ 500 × 100 = −10%

%Δ P = +£0.60 ÷ £3.00 × 100 = +20%

PED = −10% ÷ +20% = −0.5 — relatively inelastic.

Quantity fell proportionally less than price rose, so total revenue rises, from £1,500 to £1,620.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: List the determinants of PED.
cards.back:
• Number and closeness of substitutes — more substitutes, more elastic.
  • Necessity vs luxury — necessities inelastic, luxuries elastic.
  • Addictiveness — addictive goods (cigarettes) are inelastic.
  • Proportion of income — big-ticket goods are more elastic.
  • Time period — demand is more inelastic in the short run, more elastic in the long run as consumers find alternatives.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: State the formula for income elasticity of demand (YED), and the three classifications.
cards.back:
• YED above 1 — normal luxury good (income elastic), e.g. holidays.
  • YED between 0 and 1 — normal necessity (income inelastic), e.g. food.
  • YED below 0 — inferior good, e.g. budget brands, bus travel.
cards.formulaHtml: YED=%ΔQD%ΔY\text{YED} = \frac{\%\Delta Q_D}{\%\Delta Y}YED=%ΔY%ΔQD​​

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: State the formula for cross elasticity of demand (XED), and what its sign shows.
cards.back: XED above 0 — substitutes (Coke and Pepsi): a rise in the price of B raises demand for A. XED below 0 — complements (printers and ink). XED = 0 — unrelated goods. The further from zero, the stronger the relationship.
cards.formulaHtml: XED=%ΔQDA%ΔPB\text{XED} = \frac{\%\Delta Q_{D_A}}{\%\Delta P_B}XED=%ΔPB​%ΔQDA​​​

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how should a firm use PED to set prices for revenue?
cards.back:
If demand is inelastic (magnitude below 1), quantity falls proportionally less than price rises, so raising price increases total revenue. If demand is elastic (above 1), quantity responds more than proportionally, so lowering price increases revenue.

The same logic guides governments: taxing inelastic goods (cigarettes) raises revenue with only a small fall in quantity; subsidising elastic goods (green technology) triggers a large rise in consumption.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Define supply, and state the law of supply.
cards.back:
Supply — the quantity of a good/service producers are willing and able to produce/sell at a given price in a given time period.

Law of supply — a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied, ceteris paribus: higher prices raise potential profit margins, giving firms an incentive to expand output.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Distinguish a movement along the supply curve from a shift of it.
cards.back: A movement along the curve comes only from a change in the good's own price — an extension when price rises, a contraction when it falls. A shift (S1 to S2) comes from a non-price factor changing costs or capacity: production costs, indirect taxes, subsidies, technology, the number of firms in the market, or external shocks.
cards.svgAlt: Supply curve shifting right from S1 to S2, raising quantity from Q1 to Q2 at price P

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Define price elasticity of supply (PES), with its formula and value ranges.
cards.back:
PES — measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's own price: how easily, quickly or cheaply producers can increase output when the price rises.

0 = perfectly inelastic (vertical supply curve); between 0 and 1 = relatively inelastic; above 1 = relatively elastic; infinity = perfectly elastic (horizontal).
cards.formulaHtml: PES=%ΔQS%ΔP\text{PES} = \frac{\%\Delta Q_S}{\%\Delta P}PES=%ΔP%ΔQS​​

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: A t-shirt maker produces 4,000 shirts a month. Price rises from £8 to £10. In the short run output reaches 4,400; in the long run, 6,000. Calculate PES in each case.
cards.back:
%Δ P = +£2 ÷ £8 × 100 = +25%

Short run: %Δ QS = 400 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = +10%, so PES = 10 ÷ 25 = 0.4 — relatively inelastic.

Long run: %Δ QS = 2,000 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = +50%, so PES = 50 ÷ 25 = 2.0 — relatively elastic.

The identical price change gives different elasticities — time to respond is the key determinant of PES.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: List the determinants of PES, and define the short run and long run.
cards.back:
Time is the main determinant. Others: spare production capacity, ease of storing stocks, mobility of factors of production, complexity of production, the marginal cost of extra units, and the availability of raw materials.

Short run — at least one factor of production is fixed, so supply is more price inelastic. Long run — all factors are variable, so supply is more price elastic.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Define market equilibrium, the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity.
cards.back:
Market equilibrium — the point where market demand equals market supply.

The equilibrium (market-clearing) price is the price at which there is no excess demand or supply — the market clears. The equilibrium quantity is the amount bought and sold at that price.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Show excess demand on a supply and demand diagram, and how the market corrects it.
cards.back: At P1, below the equilibrium Pe, quantity demanded Qd exceeds quantity supplied Qs — the bracketed gap is the shortage. Competing buyers bid the price up (the arrows), causing an extension of supply and a contraction of demand until the market returns to Pe and Qe.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with price P1 below equilibrium Pe, showing the excess demand gap between Qs and Qd and arrows converging on equilibrium

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Show excess supply on a supply and demand diagram, and how the market corrects it.
cards.back: At P1, above the equilibrium Pe, quantity supplied Qs exceeds quantity demanded Qd — the bracketed gap is the surplus. Sellers with unsold stock cut prices (the arrows), causing a contraction of supply and an extension of demand until the market returns to Pe and Qe.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with price P1 above equilibrium Pe, showing the excess supply gap between Qd and Qs and arrows converging on equilibrium

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Predict the effect on equilibrium price and quantity of each of the four curve shifts.
cards.back:
• Demand increase (product becomes fashionable): D shifts right; excess demand at the old price; price rises to the new equilibrium — P and Q both higher.
  • Demand decrease (real incomes fall, normal good): D shifts left; excess supply; price falls — P and Q both lower.
  • Supply increase (subsidy or new technology): S shifts right; excess supply; price falls — P lower, Q higher.
  • Supply decrease (higher raw-material costs): S shifts left; excess demand; price rises — P higher, Q lower.

Naming the disequilibrium step is what earns the analysis marks.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Define joint demand and competitive demand.
cards.back:
Joint demand — two goods demanded and consumed together (complementary goods), e.g. cars and petrol: a rise in the price of cars reduces the demand for petrol.

Competitive demand — two or more goods usable for the same purpose (substitute goods), e.g. butter and margarine: a rise in the price of butter raises the demand for margarine.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Define composite demand and joint supply.
cards.back:
Composite demand — an input demanded for multiple production purposes but usable for only one at a time, e.g. milk for cheese or butter: a rise in the demand for cheese cuts the supply of butter.

Joint supply — two goods produced from the same source or process, e.g. beef and leather: a rise in the demand for beef raises the supply of leather as a by-product.

cards.topic: 1.3 Price determination in a competitive market
cards.front: Define derived demand, with an example.
cards.back:
Derived demand — when the demand for a good is determined by the demand for another good.

The demand for steel is derived from the demand for cars; the demand for bricklayers is derived from the demand for houses — a fall in house-building cuts the demand for bricklayers. AQA expects you to trace a change in one market through to its related markets.

cards.front: Define production.
cards.back:
Production: the process of combining various resources (inputs) and the factors of production to create goods and services (outputs).

Through production a business adds value — the output sells for more than the inputs cost — and production measures the total output of a firm, industry or economy over a period.

cards.front: Define productivity — and give the formula for labour productivity.
cards.back:
Productivity measures the efficiency of production: output per unit of input. Labour productivity is output per worker (or per worker per hour).

Higher productivity means lower costs per unit, higher profits and a competitive edge — which is why it recurs across the whole specification.
cards.formulaHtml: Labourproductivity=output÷numberofworkersLabour productivity = output ÷ number of workersLabourproductivity=output÷numberofworkers

cards.front: Define specialisation and the division of labour.
cards.back:
Specialisation: individuals, firms, regions or countries concentrating on producing a specific good or service — a cardiac surgeon, Tesla on electric vehicles, Silicon Valley on technology, Saudi Arabia on oil.

Division of labour splits production into separate tasks, each worker repeating one — Adam Smith's pin factory: ten specialised workers made 4,800 pins each daily, against 20 for one working alone.

cards.front: Evaluate specialisation and the division of labour.
cards.back:
For: workers get quicker and more skilled, average costs fall, and countries trading their specialisms raise global output and variety.

Against: repetitive work breeds boredom, lower quality and high staff turnover; narrow skills risk structural unemployment if the industry declines; regions become over-dependent on one product; and mass-produced goods lose variety.

cards.front: Why does specialisation require money?
cards.back:
Specialists produce one thing and need everything else, so they must trade — and barter requires a double coincidence of wants: finding someone who has what you want and wants what you have.

Money solves this as a medium of exchange, letting specialised production be swapped efficiently for everything else.

cards.front: Distinguish the short run from the long run.
cards.back:
Short run: at least one factor of production is fixed — the firm can hire more labour but its factory is a given size. Here the law of diminishing returns applies.

Long run: all factors can be varied — a bigger factory, more machinery. Here returns to scale apply. Both describe how inputs map to output, and both shape the cost curves.

cards.front: State the law of diminishing returns — and define marginal, average and total returns.
cards.back:
Marginal returns: the extra output from one more unit of a variable factor (ΔTotal output ÷ ΔInputs). Average returns: output per unit of the variable factor. Total returns: total output.

In the short run, adding a variable factor to a fixed one eventually yields smaller and smaller additions to output — more bartenders behind a fixed bar get in each other's way. This is what makes the MC curve fall and then rise.

cards.front: Define returns to scale — increasing, constant and decreasing.
cards.back:
In the long run all factors are variable, so the firm can change its whole scale. Increasing returns to scale: output rises more than proportionately to inputs. Constant: proportionately. Decreasing: less than proportionately.

Returns to scale underpin economies and diseconomies of scale — the long-run counterpart to the short run's diminishing returns.

cards.front: Define the seven cost measures and their formulas.
cards.back:
Fixed costs do not vary with output (rent, salaries); variable costs do (materials, hourly wages). TC = TFC + TVC.

The averages divide by output: AC = TC ÷ Q, AFC = TFC ÷ Q, AVC = TVC ÷ Q. MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the cost of one more unit, and the curve that drives all the others.
cards.formulaHtml: TC=TFC+TVC;AC=TC/Q;AFC=TFC/Q;AVC=TVC/Q;MC=ΔTC/ΔQTC = TFC + TVC; AC = TC/Q; AFC = TFC/Q; AVC = TVC/Q; MC = ΔTC/ΔQTC=TFC+TVC;AC=TC/Q;AFC=TFC/Q;AVC=TVC/Q;MC=ΔTC/ΔQ

cards.front: A firm has fixed costs of £150. Variable costs are £90 at 10 units, £150 at 20, £240 at 30 and £390 at 40. Calculate TC and AC at each output, and MC between each step.
cards.back:
TC = 150 + TVC: 240, 300, 390, 540

AC = TC ÷ Q: 240 ÷ 10 = £24; 300 ÷ 20 = £15; 390 ÷ 30 = £13; 540 ÷ 40 = £13.50

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ: (300 − 240) ÷ 10 = £6; then £9; then £15

AC bottoms at £13 and turns upward between 30 and 40 units — exactly where MC (£15) rises above it.

cards.front: Draw the short-run cost curves — and explain their shapes.
cards.back:
MC falls then rises — the law of diminishing returns. It cuts both AVC and AC exactly at their minimum points: whenever the marginal unit costs more than the average, the average must rise.

AFC falls continuously, because fixed costs are spread over ever more units — which is also why AC and AVC converge as output grows.
cards.svgAlt: Four short-run cost curves: a J-shaped marginal cost curve cutting average variable cost and average total cost at their minimum points, and an average fixed cost curve falling continuously

cards.front: Show the relationship between short-run and long-run average cost curves.
cards.back:
Each SRAC curve fixes a scale of plant; the LRAC is their envelope — the lowest average cost achievable at each output when everything can be varied.

In the long run the firm moves to the SRAC whose plant size suits its output, so LRAC touches each SRAC and its falling-then-rising shape reflects economies and then diseconomies of scale.
cards.svgAlt: Long-run average cost curve drawn as the envelope of several short-run average cost curves, each for a different scale of plant

cards.front: Name the six internal economies of scale.
cards.back:
Purchasing (bulk-buying discounts), technical (large-scale machinery), financial (cheaper borrowing for lower-risk large firms), managerial (specialist managers), marketing (advertising spread over more units) and risk-bearing (losses in one market offset by others).

All are reasons average total costs fall as the firm itself grows — they pull the LRAC curve down its falling arm.

cards.front: Show economies and diseconomies of scale on the LRAC curve — and mark the minimum efficient scale.
cards.back:
The falling arm of LRAC is economies of scale; the rising arm is diseconomies. The minimum efficient scale (MES) is the lowest output at which the lowest possible long-run average cost is reached.

The MES matters for market structure: where it is large relative to demand, few firms fit in the industry and entry is hard.
cards.svgAlt: U-shaped long-run average cost curve with the falling section labelled economies of scale, the rising section diseconomies of scale, and the minimum efficient scale marked at the lowest point

cards.front: What causes diseconomies of scale — and how do they differ from diminishing returns?
cards.back:
Size itself raises average costs: communication and managerial strain (messages distorted across layers), motivational problems (workers feel unnoticed — the principal-agent link) and geographical coordination across distant sites.

They are not diminishing returns: diseconomies are a long-run phenomenon of scale with all factors variable, while diminishing returns is a short-run law that needs a fixed factor.

cards.front: Define and give the formulas for total, average and marginal revenue.
cards.back: TR = P × Q, the firm's total earnings. AR = TR ÷ Q — the price per unit, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve. MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ, the extra revenue from one more unit.
cards.formulaHtml: TR=P×Q;AR=TR/Q;MR=ΔTR/ΔQTR = P × Q; AR = TR/Q; MR = ΔTR/ΔQTR=P×Q;AR=TR/Q;MR=ΔTR/ΔQ

cards.front: Show the revenue curves of a firm in perfect competition.
cards.back:
A price taker sells every unit at the market price, so D = AR = MR is one horizontal line, and TR rises at a constant rate from the origin.

Nothing the firm does changes the price — its only choice is how much to sell at it.
cards.svgAlt: Horizontal demand, average revenue and marginal revenue line at the market price with total revenue rising from the origin at a constant rate

cards.front: Show the revenue curves of a firm with market power.
cards.back:
A price maker must cut the price to sell more, so AR (the demand curve) slopes down and MR lies below it — twice as steep in the linear case, because the price cut applies to every unit, not just the last.

TR is maximised where MR = 0: beyond that output, selling more actually reduces revenue.
cards.svgAlt: Downward-sloping average revenue curve with marginal revenue below it at twice the slope, and total revenue rising to a maximum where marginal revenue is zero before falling

cards.front: A firm with market power sells 1 unit at £12, 2 at £10, 3 at £8 and 4 at £6. Calculate TR and MR at each output — where is revenue maximised?
cards.back:
TR = P × Q: £12, £20, £24, £24.

MR = ΔTR: £8, £4, £0.

Revenue peaks at £24, where MR = 0 — the fourth unit adds nothing, because the £2 price cut on the first three units exactly cancels the £6 the fourth brings in. MR falls twice as fast as price, and always sits below AR.

cards.front: Define normal profit, abnormal (supernormal) profit and loss — and state the profit-maximising rule.
cards.back:
Normal profit is the minimum profit required to keep a firm in the industry: TR = TC, the break-even point — counted as a cost, because it is the entrepreneur's opportunity cost of staying. Abnormal (supernormal) profit is anything above that (TR > TC); a loss is TR < TC.

Profit is maximised at the output where MC = MR.

cards.front: Show abnormal (supernormal) profit on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
The firm produces at Q where MC = MR, charges the price P read off AR, and has average cost C read off AC at that output.

With P above C, the shaded rectangle (P − C) × Q is abnormal profit — profit beyond the normal profit already counted inside costs.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with output at MC equals MR, the price from AR above average cost from AC, and the rectangle between them up to output Q shaded as supernormal profit

cards.front: Show a loss on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
The firm still produces where MC = MR — now the loss-minimising output. The price P comes off AR and average cost C off AC, but here C sits above P.

The shaded rectangle (C − P) × Q is the loss.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram where average cost from AC sits above the price from AR at the loss-minimising output, with the rectangle between them up to Q shaded as the loss

cards.front: What is the role of profit in a market economy?
cards.back: Profit is the market's engine: an incentive for entrepreneurs to take risks, a signal drawing resources to where they are most valued, a source of reinvestment that funds growth and innovation, a driver of competition pushing prices down and quality up, and the reward to investors for the capital they risk.

cards.front: Distinguish invention from innovation.
cards.back:
Invention: the creation of entirely new and original products, processes or ideas — the telephone.

Innovation: developing an existing product, process or idea to improve it, make it more efficient or adapt it to a new purpose — the smartphone evolving from that telephone.

cards.front: How does technological change affect production and markets?
cards.back:
It raises productivity (more output from the same inputs), improves efficiency and cuts waste, and lowers production costs — automated lines, precision agriculture.

It also reshapes markets: new products create new markets and destroy old ones — Schumpeter's creative destruction — changing market structure as innovators displace incumbents.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Describe the spectrum of competition.
cards.back: Competition refers to the number of businesses in a market and the degree of rivalry between them. The spectrum runs from perfect competition (infinitely many firms) through monopolistic competition (many) and oligopoly (a few large firms) to pure monopoly (one) — most to least competitive.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What characteristics distinguish market structures from one another?
cards.back:
The number of firms (more firms, stronger competition); whether products are homogeneous or differentiated; the height of barriers to entry and exit; and the level of information — perfect information sharpens competition, while asymmetric information dulls it.

Place any real market on the spectrum by scoring it against these four.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show profit maximisation on a firm diagram — and why is it the assumed objective?
cards.back:
Traditional theory assumes firms maximise profit, because that maximises returns to shareholders through dividends and the share price. Profit is maximised at the output Q where MC = MR: below Q each extra unit adds more revenue than cost; beyond Q the reverse.

Read the price P off the AR curve at Q and average cost C off AC — with P above C, the gap times Q is supernormal profit.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the profit-maximising point marked where MC crosses MR at output Q, price P read from AR and average cost C from AC

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show revenue maximisation on a firm diagram — and why might a firm choose it?
cards.back:
Revenue is maximised at the output where MR = 0: up to that point each extra sale still adds revenue; beyond it, the price cuts needed to sell more outweigh the extra units.

Firms choose it to build market share or reach the scale that lowers average costs — both of which can raise long-term profitability.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the revenue-maximising point marked where MR reaches zero on the quantity axis

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show sales maximisation on a firm diagram — and why might a firm choose it?
cards.back:
Sales (volume) are maximised at the largest output the firm can sustain without loss: where AC = AR, breaking even on normal profit only.

Firms choose it to grow market share, clear stock — or as limit pricing, leaving no supernormal profit on display to tempt entrants.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the sales-maximising point marked where the average cost curve crosses average revenue, so the firm breaks even

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What is the divorce of ownership and control, and what problem does it create?
cards.back:
In large firms — PLCs especially — the owners (shareholders) do not run the business day to day; they employ professional managers. Owners are the principals, managers the agents.

The principal-agent problem: managers may pursue their own objectives — salaries, perks, sales growth — instead of the owners' profit maximisation, because the separation of ownership and control leaves the two sides with different incentives and information.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What is satisficing — and what other objectives might firms pursue?
cards.back:
Satisficing: aiming for a satisfactory level of profit rather than the maximum — enough to keep shareholders content while managers meet their own goals (the principal-agent problem again), or owners protect work-life balance. Output and price settle between the profit-maximising and sales-maximising points.

Other objectives: corporate social responsibility, survival in downturns, employee welfare and wider social objectives.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Give the four characteristics of perfect competition — and what they make the firm.
cards.back:
Many buyers and sellers (each firm negligibly small), homogeneous products, perfect information, and freedom of entry and exit.

Together these make every firm a price taker: it accepts the market price as given and cannot influence it through its own actions.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show why a firm in perfect competition is a price taker.
cards.back:
The market panel sets the price: industry supply and demand cross at P1. The firm can sell any quantity at P1 and none above it, so its demand curve is perfectly elastic — horizontal at the market price.

That one line is the firm's P = MR = AR: every extra unit sells at exactly P1.
cards.svgAlt: Two panels: industry supply and demand set the market price, and the individual firm faces a horizontal demand curve at that price, so demand, average revenue and marginal revenue are the same line

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show short-run supernormal profit in perfect competition.
cards.back:
The firm produces at Q1, where MC crosses the horizontal price line (its MR). Average cost C1 at that output lies below the price, so the shaded rectangle (P1 − C1) × Q1 is supernormal profit.

It cannot last: with no barriers, entry shifts industry supply right and the market price falls.
cards.svgAlt: Perfect competition firm producing where marginal cost crosses the horizontal price line, with average cost below the price and the rectangle between them shaded as supernormal profit

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show a short-run loss in perfect competition.
cards.back:
At Q1, where MC crosses the horizontal price line, average cost C1 sits above the price: the shaded rectangle (C1 − P1) × Q1 is the loss.

Losses drive firms out; industry supply shifts left and the market price rises until the firms that remain break even again.
cards.svgAlt: Perfect competition firm where average cost lies above the horizontal price line at the output where marginal cost crosses it, with the rectangle between them shaded as the loss

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Trace the adjustment from short-run supernormal profit to long-run equilibrium in perfect competition.
cards.back:
Supernormal profit attracts new firms, which can enter freely. Industry supply shifts right, so the market price falls — and the firm's horizontal demand curve falls with it, until it is tangent to the minimum point of the AC curve. There P = AR = AC = MC and only normal profit remains.

From a short-run loss the chain runs in reverse: firms exit, supply shifts left and the price rises to the same long-run equilibrium.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Give the characteristics of monopolistic competition — and what they mean for the firm's demand curve.
cards.back:
Many firms each with a small market share, product differentiation (similar core products set apart by branding, quality, features or marketing) and low barriers to entry and exit. Think restaurants, clothing brands, hairdressers.

Differentiation gives each firm a little market power: it is a price maker facing a downward-sloping demand (AR) curve.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show the short-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition.
cards.back:
The firm maximises profit where MC = MR. In the short run it can earn supernormal profit — price read off AR above average cost read off AC, the shaded rectangle.

It can equally make a loss in the short run if AR sits below AC at that output. Neither outcome survives the long run, because entry and exit are almost free.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with output where MC equals MR and the price from AR above average cost from AC, shading supernormal profit — the short-run position available to a monopolistically competitive firm

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show the long-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition.
cards.back:
Supernormal profit attracts entrants, which take market share and shift each firm's demand curve left until only normal profit remains (losses run the same process in reverse). In long-run equilibrium AR = AC at the profit-maximising output — the AC curve is tangent to the demand curve above Q.

In the exam you may show this by shifting only the AC curve until it touches AR at that output, as here.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram where the average cost curve is tangent to the downward-sloping demand curve exactly above the output where MC equals MR, so the firm earns only normal profit

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Give the key characteristics of oligopoly.
cards.back:
A few large firms dominate (a high concentration ratio), there are high barriers to entry, products are differentiated, and — the defining feature — firms are interdependent: each must weigh rivals' likely reactions before setting price, output or marketing.

Interdependence brings strategic behaviour and uncertainty, and with them the choice between colluding and competing. Think UK supermarkets, airlines, mobile networks.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What is a concentration ratio, and how is it calculated?
cards.back:
A concentration ratio measures the degree of market concentration: the n-firm ratio is the share of total market sales held by the largest n firms. A 3-firm ratio of 80% means the top three firms account for 80% of the market's sales.

A higher ratio marks a more concentrated, generally less competitive market.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Distinguish overt and tacit collusion.
cards.back:
Collusion is firms agreeing — formally or informally — to restrict supply and raise price, acting like a monopoly to earn supernormal profit. Overt collusion is a formal agreement (a cartel): illegal and provable in court, as when British Airways and Virgin Atlantic fixed fuel surcharges in 2007.

Tacit collusion is an informal understanding, often via price leadership — the market leader sets a price and rivals follow. Same outcome, far harder to prove.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show the effect of collusion on price, output and welfare.
cards.back:
Colluding firms act like a monopoly: output is restricted to Qcoll, where MC = MR, and price rises to Pcoll — against the competitive outcome at Qcomp, where MC crosses demand (P = MC), with the lower price Pcomp.

Units between Qcoll and Qcomp that society values above their cost are no longer made: the shaded triangle between D and MC is the deadweight welfare loss from collusion.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram comparing the collusive outcome, restricted output and higher price where MC equals MR, with the competitive outcome where MC crosses demand, and the deadweight loss triangle between them shaded

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Use the kinked demand curve to explain price rigidity in a competitive oligopoly.
cards.back:
Above the current price demand is elastic: rivals ignore a price rise, so customers switch away and revenue falls. Below it demand is inelastic: rivals match a cut, so few customers arrive and revenue still falls — at worst a price war starts.

The kink makes MR discontinuous at Q, and MC can shift anywhere within the gap without changing the profit-maximising price — so prices stay "sticky" and firms compete through differentiation and advertising instead. It is one illustration of interdependence, not the only model of oligopoly.
cards.svgAlt: Demand curve kinked at the current price, elastic above and inelastic below, with a vertical gap in marginal revenue at the kink output through which the MC curve passes

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Define monopoly — pure and legal — and what gives a firm monopoly power.
cards.back:
A pure monopoly is a market structure where there is a single seller of a product with no close substitutes — a local water company. A legal (working) monopoly is defined by the CMA as 25% or more market share — Google's 90%-plus of UK search qualifies.

Monopoly power rests on high barriers to entry, few competitors, a highly differentiated product (often patent-protected) and information advantages — making the firm a price maker.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show the profit-maximising equilibrium of a monopoly.
cards.back:
The monopolist produces where MC = MR and charges the price on the demand curve above it — P > MC, with supernormal profit shaded between price and average cost.

Unlike more competitive structures, barriers to entry let this profit persist into the long run: no entrants arrive to compete it away.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with output where MC equals MR and price read from the demand curve above average cost, shading the supernormal profit a monopoly can sustain in the long run

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Assess each type of efficiency under monopoly.
cards.back:
Allocative: no — output is where MC = MR rather than AR = MC, so P > MC and there is a welfare loss to society. Productive: no — output is not at the lowest point of AC. X-inefficiency: possible — with little competition, costs may drift above their minimum.

Dynamic: yes — long-run supernormal profit gives both the means and the motive to invest in R&D, the monopolist's strongest defence.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What is a natural monopoly? Show why competition is inefficient there.
cards.back:
An industry with such a high proportion of fixed costs — water, rail, energy grids — that LRAC falls over the entire range of market demand: one firm can always supply the market more cheaply than several could.

The diagram shows the regulator's dilemma: a private profit-maximiser produces Qp at the high price Pp (grey guides), while pricing at P = MC (red guides, output Qn) is allocatively efficient but sets price below average cost, a loss needing subsidy.
cards.svgAlt: Natural monopoly diagram with long-run average cost falling over the whole market and marginal cost below it: private profit maximisation gives low output and a high price, while pricing at marginal cost gives high output but a price below average cost

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Name and define the three degrees of price discrimination.
cards.back: Price discrimination is charging different consumers different prices for the same product, where the differences do not reflect costs. First-degree: each consumer pays the maximum they are willing to — auctions — capturing all consumer surplus. Second-degree: prices vary by quantity or version — bulk discounts, premium tiers. Third-degree: different consumer groups pay different prices by age, location or time of use — train tickets.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What three conditions make third-degree price discrimination possible?
cards.back:
(1) Market power, so few or no substitutes; (2) sub-markets with different PEDs the firm can identify — peak against off-peak travel, student against adult tickets; (3) the ability to separate the markets and prevent resale (arbitrage), often through ID.

Meeting all three lets the firm turn one price into several — and more of the consumer surplus into profit.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show how third-degree price discrimination raises a monopolist's profit.
cards.back:
In each sub-market the firm sells where MR = MC and reads the price off that group's demand curve: the inelastic group (steep D — peak travellers) pays the high price; the elastic group (flatter D — off-peak) pays less.

The two shaded rectangles together exceed the single-price profit, because pricing by group captures more consumer surplus. Inelastic-demand customers pay more and lose surplus; elastic-demand customers pay less and gain; and the extra profit can fund R&D — the firm's standard defence.
cards.svgAlt: Two panels sharing one horizontal AC equals MC line: the steep inelastic sub-market pays a high price and the flatter elastic sub-market a lower one, with each group's profit rectangle shaded

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What are the short-run and long-run benefits of competition?
cards.back:
Short run: immediately lower prices as firms undercut, wider choice, and non-price competition — advertising, branding, differentiation.

Long run: sustained lower prices as firms cut costs to survive, and lasting quality improvements as R&D becomes the way to stay ahead. Competition disciplines firms on every margin, not just price.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What is creative destruction?
cards.back:
Creative destruction is a process in which new innovations and technologies replace older ones, leading to the destruction of existing businesses and industries — digital photography destroying Kodak's film business.

It is fundamental to how competition works: monopoly profits attract entrants who innovate over the barriers, so today's dominant firm is always exposed to tomorrow's better idea.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: What is a contestable market — and how does contestability differ from competition?
cards.back:
A contestable market is one with freedom of entry and exit. What disciplines firms is the threat of potential competition, not the number of firms currently in the market.

The distinction: competition is about how many firms there are; contestability is about how easily firms can enter and leave. A concentrated market can still behave competitively if it is highly contestable.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Give the characteristics of a contestable market — and the role of sunk costs.
cards.back:
No (or very low) barriers to entry and exit, minimal sunk costs, no competitive disadvantage for entrants, and perfect information — together making hit-and-run competition possible: enter, take the short-run supernormal profit, leave when it is competed back to normal.

Sunk costs — unrecoverable on exit (specialised machinery, advertising, R&D) — are the key barrier: the higher they are, the riskier entry becomes and the less contestable the market.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show limit pricing — how an incumbent deters entry in a contestable market.
cards.back:
Rather than profit-maximising at MC = MR, the incumbent sets price down at the output where AR = AC, earning only normal profit — the same point a sales-maximiser chooses.

With no supernormal profit on display, there is no profit signal to attract entrants. The more contestable the market, the closer behaviour drifts towards the perfectly competitive outcome.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the chosen point at the output where average revenue equals average cost, so only normal profit is earned and no supernormal profit remains to attract new entrants

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Define the four types of efficiency — and static efficiency.
cards.back:
Allocative: production where AR = MC — the optimal mix of goods for society. Productive: production at minimum AC, where MC = AC. Dynamic: long-run supernormal profits reinvested in R&D improve products and costs over time. X-inefficiency: without competitive pressure, costs drift above their minimum.

Static efficiency: resources both allocated and utilised in the most efficient way possible at a given point in time — requiring allocative and productive efficiency together.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show efficiency in perfect competition in long-run equilibrium.
cards.back:
The horizontal price line is tangent to the minimum of AC, and MC passes through the same point: P = MC gives allocative efficiency and minimum AC gives productive efficiency, both at the same output Q.

But with only normal profit there is nothing to reinvest, so dynamic efficiency is unlikely.
cards.svgAlt: Perfect competition long-run diagram with the horizontal price line tangent to the minimum of the average cost curve where marginal cost also crosses, marking the productively and allocatively efficient points at the same output

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show why a firm with market power is allocatively and productively inefficient.
cards.back:
Profit-maximising at MC = MR, the firm stops short of both efficient points: P > MC, so there is allocative inefficiency — underproduction and a deadweight welfare loss — and output lies left of minimum AC, so there is productive inefficiency.

But P > AC means supernormal profit that can be reinvested in R&D — the potential for dynamic efficiency.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with market power producing where MC equals MR, short of both the productively efficient point at minimum average cost and the allocatively efficient point where demand crosses marginal cost, with supernormal profit shaded

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Evaluate: is perfect competition more efficient than imperfect competition?
cards.back:
Statically, yes: long-run equilibrium is both allocatively and productively efficient, while a firm with market power is neither — and, shielded from competition, it may drift into X-inefficiency.

Dynamically, the ranking can reverse: only supernormal profit sustained into the long run funds R&D and innovation, and perfect competition competes that profit away. The trade-off is static efficiency today against dynamic efficiency tomorrow.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Define consumer surplus and producer surplus.
cards.back:
Consumer surplus — the difference between what a consumer is willing to pay (their valuation) and what they actually pay. A measure of consumer welfare.

Producer surplus — the difference between the price a producer is willing to accept (their cost of supply) and the price they actually receive. A measure of producer welfare.

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Show consumer and producer surplus on a supply and demand diagram.
cards.back: Consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price line; producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price line. Their sum is the social (community) surplus — total welfare — and it is maximised at the free-market equilibrium: any move away from it creates a welfare loss.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with consumer surplus shaded between the demand curve and the price line and producer surplus between the price line and the supply curve

cards.topic: 1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly
cards.front: Apply surplus analysis: what happens to consumer and producer surplus under monopoly and under price discrimination?
cards.back:
Monopoly restricts output and raises price: consumer surplus shrinks, part transfers to producer surplus, and the rest becomes a deadweight welfare loss — the application AQA names in the specification.

Price discrimination converts consumer surplus into producer surplus: inelastic customers pay more and lose surplus, elastic customers pay less and gain, and overall consumer surplus falls.

cards.front: Define the demand for labour — and why is it a derived demand?
cards.back:
Demand for labour: the quantity of workers that firms are willing and able to employ at a given wage rate.

It is a derived demand because labour demand is derived from the demand for the goods and services that labour helps to produce — firms hire workers for what they make, not for their own sake.

cards.front: State the marginal revenue product formula — and define its parts.
cards.back:
MRP = MPP × MR. Marginal physical product (MPP): the extra output produced by one more worker. Marginal revenue (MR): the extra revenue gained from selling that extra output.

The MRP curve is the demand curve for labour, D(L), and it slopes downward because of the law of diminishing returns.
cards.formulaHtml: MRP=MPP×MRMRP = MPP × MRMRP=MPP×MR

cards.front: A firm sells output at a constant £6 per unit. Total output is 15 with one worker, 34 with two, 49 with three and 58 with four. Calculate each worker's MRP — and how many workers are hired at a wage of £60?
cards.back:
MPP: 15, 19, 15, 9. MRP = MPP × £6: £90, £114, £90, £54.

Hire while MRP is at least the wage: the third worker adds £90 (≥ £60) but the fourth only £54 (< £60), so the firm employs three workers. MPP rising to the second worker then falling is the law of diminishing returns setting in — the reason the MRP curve, and so labour demand, slopes downward.

cards.front: Show the demand curve for labour.
cards.back:
The curve D(L) = MRP plots the marginal revenue product of each extra worker against the wage. It slopes downward because of the law of diminishing returns: as more workers are hired, MPP typically falls.

A wage change moves the firm along the curve — at W1 it hires Q1, at the lower W2 it hires Q2 — while anything changing MRP itself shifts the whole curve.
cards.svgAlt: Downward-sloping labour demand curve labelled D of L equals MRP, with a high wage W1 giving employment Q1 and a lower wage W2 giving the larger employment Q2

cards.front: What shifts the demand curve for labour?
cards.back:
Anything that changes labour's MRP: higher demand for the final product (the derived-demand link) or a higher price of the final product raises MRP and shifts D(L) right, and higher labour productivity does the same through MPP.

Substitutability works the other way: if capital becomes a better substitute for labour, the demand for labour shifts left.

cards.front: What determines the wage elasticity of demand for labour?
cards.back:
Labour demand is more elastic when the final product's demand is price elastic, when capital can easily substitute for labour, and when labour is a high proportion of total costs — so a wage change moves total costs significantly.

It is also more elastic in the long run, when firms have had time to reorganise production.

cards.front: Define the supply of labour — and what draws workers into one occupation over another?
cards.back:
Supply of labour: the quantity of workers willing and able to work at a given wage rate. For a market or occupation the curve slopes upward — higher wages encourage more workers to enter the job.

Workers weigh monetary considerations — the wage, bonuses, overtime — against non-monetary considerations such as working conditions, flexible hours and other benefits.

cards.front: What shifts the supply curve of labour to an occupation?
cards.back: A change in any factor other than the wage that affects willingness or ability to do the job: monetary benefits (stock options, bonuses, overtime pay), non-monetary benefits (working conditions, flexible hours, healthcare), demographic change and migration policy (the size of the available workforce), education and training (who is qualified to do it), and taxation and welfare benefits (the incentive to work at all).

cards.front: How does labour immobility cause labour market failure — and which policies improve mobility?
cards.back:
Geographical immobility — workers cannot move easily to where the jobs are (high house prices and rent, expensive transport, lack of information). Occupational immobility — skills do not match the jobs available (few transferable skills, training and qualification requirements, technological change). Both cause structural unemployment and skill shortages.

Policies: education, training, apprenticeships and career guidance for occupational mobility; subsidised housing, relocation assistance, better transport and job information for geographical.

cards.front: What determines the wage elasticity of supply of labour?
cards.back:
Supply responds more to a wage change over a longer time period (time to retrain or move), where workers are occupationally and geographically mobile, where substitute workers are available, and where there is a large pool of unemployed labour to draw on.

It is less elastic for vocational occupations requiring specific skills or qualifications — a pay rise cannot recruit surgeons this year.

cards.front: Show wage determination in a perfectly competitive labour market.
cards.back:
Many firms demand labour and many workers supply it, so both sides are wage takers: they accept the market equilibrium wage. The equilibrium wage W1 and employment Q1 sit where D(L) = MRP crosses S(L) = AC.

This is the benchmark that monopsony, trade unions and the minimum wage all depart from.
cards.svgAlt: Labour market diagram with the upward-sloping labour supply curve and downward-sloping labour demand curve crossing at the equilibrium wage W1 and employment Q1

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how do market forces return a competitive labour market to equilibrium?
cards.back:
Wage above equilibrium: excess supply of labour — a surplus of workers — so workers reduce their wage demands to enter employment, and the wage falls back to equilibrium.

Wage below equilibrium: excess demand for labour — a shortage of workers — so firms compete for workers by offering higher wages, and the wage rises until the shortage closes at equilibrium.

cards.front: What makes a labour market imperfectly competitive — and what is a monopsony?
cards.back:
Three main causes: monopsony power (a single or dominant buyer of labour with wage-setting power), trade unions (workers' collective bargaining power, backed by the threat of industrial action) and imperfect information (workers do not know all wage rates and job opportunities, so make suboptimal employment decisions).

A monopsony is a single or dominant buyer of labour — the NHS in the UK healthcare labour market — able to pay workers less than their MRP.

cards.front: Show how a monopsony sets wages and employment.
cards.back:
The monopsonist faces the entire labour supply curve (S = AC): hiring one more worker means raising pay for existing workers too, so MCL lies above supply. It hires Qm, where MCL = MRP, and with wage-setting power pays only Wm — the lowest wage workers will accept, read off the supply curve.

Compared with the competitive outcome (Wc, Qc), a monopsony employs fewer workers at a lower wage.
cards.svgAlt: Monopsony labour market diagram with the marginal cost of labour rising above the supply curve, employment set where MCL crosses MRP, and the wage read off the supply curve below the competitive wage and employment

cards.front: What is a trade union — and how is union density calculated?
cards.back:
Trade union: an organisation formed by workers to protect their rights, improve pay and secure better working conditions — using collective bargaining backed by the threat of industrial action.

Union density — union members as a proportion of the total workforce — measures its power over the employer, alongside the size of the union, the firm's profitability, the state of the economy and the stance of government policy.

cards.front: Show a trade union entering a competitive labour market.
cards.back:
The union negotiates W(TU) above the equilibrium W1. At that wage employers hire only Qd, while Qs workers want jobs: employment falls from Q1 to Qd, and the unemployment created is real wage unemployment.

Members who keep their jobs win higher pay; the cost falls on those priced out of work.
cards.svgAlt: Labour market diagram with a trade union wage set above equilibrium, cutting employment to Qd while Qs workers seek jobs, the gap being real wage unemployment

cards.front: Show a trade union facing a monopsony employer.
cards.back:
Union against monopsonist is a bilateral monopoly: a single seller of labour meets a single buyer. The negotiated W(TU) flattens the effective cost of labour out to Qc — hiring another worker no longer raises everyone's pay — so the profit-maximising hire rises from Qm to Qc while the wage rises from Wm to W(TU).

Countering monopsony power, a union can raise both wages and employment.
cards.svgAlt: Monopsony labour market with a union wage drawn as a flat line out to Qc, then a vertical jump up to the original marginal cost of labour, raising both the wage and employment compared with the monopsony outcome

cards.front: Show the impact of a national minimum wage on a labour market.
cards.back:
National minimum wage (NMW): a legally enforced price floor set above the market equilibrium wage. The floor at Wmin raises the wages of lower income earners from W1, reducing income inequality — but demand for labour contracts from Q1 to QD while supply extends to QS.

The surplus QS − QD is real wage unemployment: higher pay for those in work, fewer of them employed.
cards.svgAlt: Labour market diagram with a national minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage, contracting labour demand to QD, extending labour supply to QS, the gap being unemployment

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of a national minimum wage.
cards.back:
Depends on its size: far above equilibrium, it raises incomes significantly but creates substantial real wage unemployment. Depends on the wage elasticity of labour demand: with elastic demand the job losses are larger — the NMW works best where demand is wage inelastic.

And depends on motivation: if higher pay makes workers more productive, the rise in firms' average costs is offset and fewer jobs are lost.

cards.front: Define discrimination and wage discrimination in the labour market.
cards.back:
Discrimination: the unfair treatment of individuals based on characteristics such as gender, ethnicity, age, or disability, rather than their abilities or qualifications.

Wage discrimination — economics' main concern — is when workers with similar skills and qualifications are paid differently based on characteristics unrelated to their job performance, such as gender, ethnicity, or age.

cards.front: What conditions are necessary for wage discrimination to occur?
cards.back: Monopsony power — employers control the labour market enough to set wages below competitive levels. Information asymmetry — workers cannot see wage rates and opportunities, so cannot negotiate fair pay, and firms exploit this by offering some groups less. Bias and prejudice — employers hold discriminatory attitudes towards certain groups. Lack of regulation — insufficient legislation and enforcement lets discriminatory pay stand.

cards.front: What are the main forms and impacts of wage discrimination?
cards.back:
The gender wage gap and the ethnic wage gap — differences in average earnings between men and women, and between ethnic groups.

Impacts: reduced income and living standards for discriminated workers; reduced employment and fewer opportunities to advance, entrenching inequality; and economic inefficiency — employers who do not hire the most qualified candidates misallocate resources, lowering productivity and growth.

cards.topic: 1.7 The distribution of income and wealth: poverty and inequality
cards.front: Distinguish income inequality from wealth inequality.
cards.back:
Income inequality: the unequal distribution of earnings, such as wages, rent, interest, and profit. Income is a flow of money over a period of time.

Wealth inequality: the unequal distribution of assets, such as property, shares, and savings. Wealth is a stock of monetary value at a point in time.

cards.topic: 1.7 The distribution of income and wealth: poverty and inequality
cards.front: Show how the Lorenz curve illustrates inequality.
cards.back:
The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentage of total income or wealth against the cumulative percentage of the population. The 45° diagonal is the line of perfect equality — everyone has the same; the Lorenz curve shows the actual distribution.

The further the curve bows from the diagonal, the greater the inequality. Area A (between the two) against area A + B (everything under the diagonal) gives the Gini coefficient.
cards.svgAlt: Lorenz curve diagram with a 45 degree line of perfect equality, the Lorenz curve bowing below it, area A between the two lines and area B beneath the Lorenz curve

cards.topic: 1.7 The distribution of income and wealth: poverty and inequality
cards.front: How is the Gini coefficient calculated from the Lorenz curve — and how is it read?
cards.back:
Gini coefficient = A ÷ (A + B): the area between the line of perfect equality and the Lorenz curve (A), as a ratio of the total area under the line of perfect equality (A + B).

0 means perfect equality, 1 means perfect inequality — so a higher Gini coefficient means greater inequality. AQA asks you to interpret the coefficient, not calculate it from data.
